To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(A) resolution based algorithms are not likely to yield good approximations to independent set, clique and vertex cover, (B) clause learning can be analyzed as a resolution proof system and is a useful refinement, and (C) SAT solvers can be made more efficient by exploiting high level problem structure.

(1) Resolution lower bound techniques can be used to derive hardness of approximation results, (2) Clause learning is a special case of a general technique called variable order resolution and (3) Structure aware SAT solvers can achieve speed ups of several orders of magnitude over state of the art solvers.

(i) there is a close connection between resolution proof size and the quality of approximation algorithms, (ii) the proof system framework provides a natural and powerful way of analyzing SAT solvers, and (iii) the SAT solver community can benefit greatly from incorporating high level problem descriptions in the search procedure.

developing a deeper understanding of proof systems in order to derive algorithmic applications.
the design and analysis of algorithms for solving hard problems, both in the worst case and in the average case.
the design of new proof complexity techniques and their application to algorithmic problems in the context of automated reasoning.
